raw.summary: Active Support: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize
raw.details:
### Impact
When constant lookup raises `LoadError`, `ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize` (and `String#safe_constantize`) builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application unavailable.

Action Cable passes the `channel` value of each `subscribe` command to `safe_constantize` before any channel lookup, so in the default configuration an unauthenticated client of the Action Cable endpoint can reach this code.

### Details
The check that decides whether `safe_constantize` returns `nil` or re-raises the `LoadError` now matches the first segment of the constant name against the error message as a literal string, and no longer compiles a regular expression. It returns the same result as before for constant names that contain no regular expression syntax.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Mounts Action Cable, which a new Rails application does by default at `/cable` (`config.action_cable.mount_path`), or otherwise passes untrusted input to `safe_constantize`.
- Accepts Action Cable connections from untrusted clients. `ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` authenticates nobody unless the application adds a check.

### Workarounds
Applications that do not use Action Cable can set `config.action_cable.mount_path = nil` to remove the endpoint. Applications that use Action Cable can call `reject_unauthorized_connection` in `ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` for unauthenticated clients, which limits exposure to authenticated users but does not remove it.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/95aa9e416016524956d4904fed96eaed079580bb.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/210ac22d446c8e2625b091e79256806b836eee20.patch

### Versions affected

- activesupport < 8.0.5.2
- activesupport >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by Felix Tscheulin ([flixt](https://hackerone.com/flixt)) through HackerOne researcher [scheja](https://hackerone.com/scheja), and independently by Bucky Wolfe ([Igneous](https://github.com/Igneous)), who provided a proof of concept that crashes the server. It was also found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-ZUN5KU3Q).

raw.summary: pgEdge Go LLM Library discloses provider API key fragments in error messages
raw.details:
### Impact

An unauthenticated caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The library's own health handler pings every configured provider using the operator's real credential and returns the resulting error text verbatim. Providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected, so a failing ping published a fragment of
the key.

**The endpoint is unauthenticated by default.** `authorize()` returns
true immediately when the consuming application sets no `Authorize` hook,
so `GET /v1/health` is reachable by anyone who can reach the listening
port unless the consumer opted in to authentication.

**Who is affected:** any application embedding pgedge-go-llm-lib at
`0.1.0` or `0.1.1` that exposes the bundled HTTP proxy without setting an
`Authorize` hook. Both affected versions are released tags and resolve
through the public Go module proxy.

The disclosed material authenticates to a **third-party provider
account** rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity
carries Scope: Changed.

Evidence at `v0.1.1`: `llm/proxy/handlers.go:296` (`handleHealth`
returning `err.Error()` in `ProviderHealth.Error`), `llm/proxy/proxy.go:247`
(`authorize()` defaulting to permit), and `llm/proxy/proxy.go:350`
(`writeError` writing the error with no redaction).

### Patches

**Fixed in `0.2.0`. Upgrade to `0.2.0` or later**, which redacts
credentials from provider error messages unconditionally. The fix adds
`llm/internal/redact`, with a follow-up anchoring word boundaries, and is
pinned by tests in that package.

**Note the version.** There is no `0.1.2` — it was never cut, and some
earlier material named it in error. `0.2.0` is the first fixed release.

**Upgrading does not undo a disclosure that already happened. Rotate any
LLM provider credential configured on an affected version** where the
proxy was reachable without an `Authorize` hook, particularly if a
provider was rejecting that key at the time.

### Workarounds

Set an `Authorize` hook on the proxy, which closes the unauthenticated
route to the health endpoint. Restricting network access to the listening
port limits who can reach it. Neither removes the underlying disclosure
for a caller who does reach the endpoint.

raw.summary: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
raw.details:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both `parse()` and `_parse`. Its `parse()` runs `initialize()` followed by a `while self.step() is not None` loop that never enters the guarded base `_parse`. Its `_parse` override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited `self._parse_deadline` or `self._max_time`. Its `__init__` signature omits `max_time` entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.

```text
Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser
- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)
- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)
- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)
Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150
```

## Impact

An actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes `parse()` can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input deterministically consumes a CPU core. In a deployment that parses attacker-influenced input on a bounded worker pool, repeated requests exhaust the pool and deny service to legitimate users. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required in that worst-credible deployment. Exploitation requires that the target actually use this parser on untrusted input; because the stepping parser is primarily a debugging or interactive-stepping component that backs a GUI, real-world exposure is narrower than for the base parser, though `parse()` is a supported public method that behaves as a full parser.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the nltk package (3.10.3) and standard library; no data downloads or network access.`

Reproduction steps:
1. Build an ambiguous, self-embedding grammar such as `S -> 'a' S S | 'a'`.
2. Confirm the base parser self-terminates: `RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a']*17)` raises `TimeoutError` at about 2 seconds.
3. Run the stepping parser on the same grammar and input and observe it never returns.

```python
import time, inspect
from nltk import CFG
from nltk.parse.recursivedescent import RecursiveDescentParser, SteppingRecursiveDescentParser

g = CFG.fromstring("S -> 'a' S S | 'a'")

# Base parser is bounded and self-terminates.
try:
    list(RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a'] * 17))
except TimeoutError:
    print("base: TimeoutError (guarded)")

# Stepping subclass cannot be bounded: no max_time parameter.
print("stepping __init__ sig:", inspect.signature(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.__init__))

# Stepping parser runs unbounded on the same input.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
list(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser(g).parse(['a'] * 17))  # does not return
print("stepping: returned after", time.perf_counter() - t0)
```

```text
base: TimeoutError (guarded)
stepping __init__ sig: (self, grammar, trace=0)
# stepping len3: 1 parse in 0.001s ; len7: 5 in 0.017s ; len9: 14 in 0.075s ; len11: 42 in 0.36s
# stepping len17: still running past a 10s watchdog, process alive, no RecursionError
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A caller uses `nltk.parse.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser`, a public exported symbol (`nltk/parse/__init__.py:97`), invoking `parse(tokens)` on grammar and input influenced by an actor.
2. **Control:** The actor influences the grammar (an ambiguous, self-embedding CFG such as `S -> 'a' S S | 'a'`) and supplies a short token list (for example 17 copies of `'a'`). Both survive to the parser unchanged.
3. **Path:** `parse()` (`recursivedescent.py:428`) calls `initialize()` then loops `while self.step() is not None`; `step()` (`:479`) calls `match()`/`expand()` (`:552`/`:512`) which call the inherited `_match`/`_expand` (`:172`/`:214`), which resolve `self._parse` by MRO to the subclass stub (`:643`).
4. **Guard:** The `max_time` wall-clock deadline exists only in the base `_parse` (`:141-150`) and is never entered on this path; the stub `_parse` records state and returns without consulting the deadline, and `__init__` exposes no `max_time` to enable a bound.
5. **Primitive:** The unbounded top-down search enumerates a Catalan-number-sized derivation space with no memoization and no deadline.
6. **Result:** The `parse()` call never returns and pins a CPU core; repeated calls exhaust a bounded worker pool, denying service.

## Bypass Evidence

The prior fix for this class of issue added a `max_time` wall-clock deadline to the base `RecursiveDescentParser._parse` (`recursivedescent.py:141-150`, default 5.0 seconds). This report demonstrates that the fix does not cover the sibling `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` entry point, and the maintainers separately hardened other parsers (chart, earley chart, viterbi, shift-reduce, non-projective dependency) with `max_time` while leaving this subclass unbounded.

Challenges attempted and their outcomes:
- Hypothesis that the inherited `self._max_time` value (observed at 5.0) makes the path guarded: refuted; the value is inherited but never read on the stepping path, and the parser runs unbounded despite it being set.
- Hypothesis that a caller can bound the parser via the constructor: refuted; `inspect.signature(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.__init__)` is `(self, grammar, trace=0)`, with no `max_time` parameter.
- Hypothesis that the failure is merely an early `RecursionError` rather than CPU exhaustion: refuted; the step loop is iterative over an explicit history stack, so no exception is raised within a 10 second watchdog, CPU time grows exponentially with input length, and a small negative control input returns in about 0.001 seconds.
- Hypothesis that the `_tried_e`/`_tried_m` records collapse the search: refuted; those records are keyed by the frozen full partial tree, so they deduplicate only identical productions at identical states and do not prevent the exponential enumeration.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI sdist nltk-3.10.3.tar.gz)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The stepping subclass has never carried a time or step bound in any released version; the prior fix added the guard only to the base class. The vulnerable methods were verified present in the exact published PyPI 3.10.3 source distribution (`parse()` at lines 428-433, stub `_parse` at 643-668 with no deadline reference, and `__init__` without `max_time`). Because the class predates the prior fix and no specific historical introduction tag was pinned, the lower bound is left open rather than invented; the upper bound is verified against the current published artifact (3.10.3). No released fix exists.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a bounded parse on the stepping parser: give `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` its own wall-clock or step-count budget that is checked inside its step loop (for example in `parse()` and/or the `_parse`/`step` path), and add a `max_time` (or equivalent step-limit) parameter to `__init__` that is propagated and honored, mirroring the base `RecursiveDescentParser` and the other hardened sibling parsers. As an interim mitigation without a code change, callers should avoid invoking `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` on grammars or input derived from untrusted sources, run any such parsing under an external timeout or a separate resource-limited process, and prefer a chart parser for untrusted input.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144.

Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)" (SteppingRecursiveDescentParser gains the max_time parameter, default 5.0 s, and honours the parse deadline).

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run (grammar S -> 'a' S S | 'a', 17 tokens): on the PR head the parse raises TimeoutError after 5.0 s and the constructor signature is (self, grammar, trace=0, max_time=5.0); on develop 2fa3f48fe the same parse ran past a 45 s watchdog, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

Release: none.

raw.summary: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
raw.details:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

### Proof of concept

```ruby
require "addressable/uri"
require "uri"

url = "http://example.com/../../public/x/../../secret"

# Addressable's normalized path, compared with RFC 3986 resolution by Ruby's URI library
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path
puts URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path

# join and == use the same normalization
puts Addressable::URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url) == Addressable::URI.parse("http://example.com/public/x/secret")

# An allowlist check on the normalized path passes, but the request reaches /secret
def allowed?(url) = Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path.start_with?("/public/")
puts allowed?(url)
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.0:

```
/public/x/secret
/secret
/public/x/secret
true
true
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.1:

```
/secret
/secret
/secret
false
false
```


### Impact

This is an interpretation conflict (CWE-436) between Addressable and other RFC 3986 resolvers, which could lead to path traversal past an allowlist (CWE-22). An application is affected when it does both of these:

- makes an access decision on a path normalized or joined by Addressable, such as "only paths under `/public/` may be proxied" or "only these redirect targets are allowed";
- sends the original, unnormalized URI to a component that resolves dot segments itself, such as an HTTP client, a proxy, a web server or a browser.

An attacker may be able to bypass a check by exploiting behavioral differences between URI parsers. Impact from this is application-dependent. Applications that use Addressable's normalized form for both the check and the request are unaffected, as are applications that reject paths containing `..` segments.

As a work-around for unpatched versions, before making access decisions on a path, either reject any containing `..` segments, including percent-encoded forms such as `%2e%2e`, or use the same normalized value for both the check and the request.

raw.summary: compose-lint: File paths embedded in pull requests can inject CI workflow commands through command-line error messages
raw.details:
### Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. The fix escapes the command openers in compose-lint's own output, but not in the argument parser's error messages. When a repository path reaches compose-lint's arguments without a `--` before it, the argument parser prints it raw in its error message. That includes a carriage return, which the runner treats as a line break, so a command can also start a new line there.

A pull request can therefore create annotations, fold or hide parts of the job log, or issue other commands the runner accepts, when CI runs compose-lint over it, before anyone reviews it. The pass/fail result is not changed.

Affected setups pass repository paths to compose-lint without a `--` before them: the pre-commit hook when `args:` is set without the documented trailing `--`, or the `compose-lint` package or Docker image called that way in a workflow. The pre-commit hook's default configuration passes `--` and is not affected. The GitHub Action turns command processing off around each compose-lint run, so it is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review. It was first published as part of GHSA-r7j4-crjv-h467, together with four other gaps in the same fix. Each gap now has its own advisory.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tag 0.31.0 and the matching minor tag are affected, as was `latest` while it pointed to 0.31.0.

Releases before 0.31.0 are covered by GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. The argument parser's messages go through the same sanitizer as the rest of compose-lint's output.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
- End the pre-commit hook's `args:` with `--`, and put `--` before file paths when calling compose-lint directly.
- On GitHub Actions, use the `tmatens/compose-lint` Action, or bracket the compose-lint step with `::stop-commands::<random token>` and `::<token>::`, as the Action does.

### Reproduction

On compose-lint 0.31.0 on a GitHub-hosted runner (runner 2.337.0), `compose-lint '--##[warning]X/compose.yml'` with no `--` creates an annotation. The same path after `--` creates none. The `composelint/compose-lint:0.31.0` image produces byte-identical output to the package.

raw.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
raw.details:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, is not affected. `to_ascii` and `normalized_host` are not affected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.0.0, the first version with the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, when that implementation is in use. It is fixed in 2.9.1, where such labels are returned unchanged, as with libidn.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation.
- Don't make security decisions on `display_uri` or `to_unicode` output. Compare hosts using `normalized_host`.

### Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with multiple variables
raw.details:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such as `http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref}` needs about 2 KB of input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. The second form, many-variable `+` and `#` expressions, is also exploitable on MRI Ruby 3.2, which does not memoize a regular expression that contains possessive quantifiers, and 2.9.0 generates those for these operators. It is also exploitable on TruffleRuby 40.0, whose regular expression engine falls back to backtracking for them. MRI Ruby 3.3 and later are not affected by any form, because they memoize those regular expressions too. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected by the other two forms. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| JRuby 10.1 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Vulnerable |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.3 or later, if a consuming application does not use JRuby or TruffleRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates with several variables in one expression, or with several expressions next to each other.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations
raw.details:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include an SVG reference element such as `use`, along with `href` or `xlink:href` in the allowed attributes. The default allowed tags include no SVG elements, so the default configuration is not affected. Applications that use Loofah directly are exposed through its own copy of the check, fixed in Loofah 2.25.3.

## Workarounds

Run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time, or remove the SVG reference elements from the overridden allowed tags.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
raw.details:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick`, which is the default for applications on `load_defaults 6.1` or earlier.
- Runs ImageMagick under a security policy that does not already deny the coders involved. The policies that Debian and Ubuntu package do not.
- Allows file uploads from untrusted users.

### Mitigation
- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.
- An application whose variant processor is `:mini_magick` must use mini_magick `>= 5.1`, which applying the policy requires. With an older mini_magick, such an application raises an exception during boot.
- An application that renders PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must re-allow the `gs` delegate and the coders it uses in the host's `policy.xml`.
- An application that replaces `MiniMagick.cli_env` after boot, clears the environment with `MiniMagick.cli_prefix`, or installs its own `MiniMagick::Shell` does not receive the shipped policy and must carry its rules in ImageMagick's system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.
- If attachments are stored with the Disk service, change `secret_key_base` and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything `config/credentials.yml.enc` holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not retain an exposed secret as a fallback.

### Workarounds
Copy the rules of the policy that the fixed versions ship, `activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml`, into ImageMagick's system policy, for example `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. At a minimum, deny the `MSL` coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the `gs` delegate:

```xml
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="MSL"/>
<policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="gs"/>
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="{PS,PS2,PS3,EPS,EPS2,EPS3,EPI,EPSF,EPSI,EPT,EPT2,EPT3,PDF,AI,EPDF,PDFA,POCKETMOD,XPS,PCL}"/>
```

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/468aa9a93fc98f5476b6821770f4ccfcb7f7d328
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ea8c40121ce53a3d0255cd4eb6d13bfe3bc01776

### Versions affected
- activestorage < 8.0.5.2
- activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [ryotak](https://hackerone.com/ryotak).

### References
- ImageMagick [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/security-policy/)

raw.summary: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/svelte
raw.details:
## Summary The `@astrojs/svelte` renderer wraps slotted content passed to Svelte components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.svelte'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Svelte 5 component that renders its snippets by name: ```svelte {@render snippets[active]?.()} ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Svelte component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Svelte component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means a Svelte 5 component that renders snippets by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/svelte` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. The same unescaped value was also used when hydrating the component in the browser. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/svelte` >= 5.7.3, <= 9.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer and in the client-side hydration code. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

raw.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
raw.details:
## Summary

`TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example `'"' * n`), it performs a `list.pop(0)` operation once per quote token, and because `list.pop(0)` is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

Inside `span_tokenize`, when the input contains double or repeated quotes, the code builds `matched`, a list with one entry per quote occurrence, and then reconstructs tokens in a comprehension that calls `matched.pop(0)` for each token that is a quote. Removing the first element of a Python list is an O(len(list)) operation because all remaining elements are shifted. For an all-quote input the tokenizer produces n quote tokens and `matched` has n entries, so `pop(0)` is called n times, each time on a list of shrinking but still linear length, giving cumulative O(n^2) CPU work. The violated invariant is bounded per-input work: there is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or the underlying `tokenize`, so untrusted input length translates into quadratic processing time. The neighboring `align_tokens` call is linear and is not the quadratic term.

```text
Affected function: TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/treebank.py
  - branch selector at line 203
  - matched list built at line 205
  - quadratic sink matched.pop(0) at line 209
  - linear align_tokens call at line 215
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls text passed to `TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release, an all-quote input of 128,000 characters takes about 1.76 seconds and 256,000 characters about 6.57 seconds on a single core, with cost growing as the square of the length. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion producing denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that uses span tokenization on untrusted input, such as offset, annotation, or highlighting pipelines. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is worker-pool exhaustion; this is inferred from the measured per-request cost and was not executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed.`

1. Instantiate `TreebankWordTokenizer`.
2. Call `span_tokenize` on an all-double-quote string of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against an equal-token-count control input that avoids the quote branch.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import TreebankWordTokenizer

tok = TreebankWordTokenizer()
for n in (32000, 64000, 128000, 256000):
    payload = '"' * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    list(tok.span_tokenize(payload))
    print("quote-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "a " * 128000  # comparable token count, avoids the pop(0) branch
start = time.perf_counter()
list(tok.span_tokenize(control))
print("control", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
quote-run 32000 0.23
quote-run 64000 0.52
quote-run 128000 1.76
quote-run 256000 6.57   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 0.16            (roughly 11x faster, isolates pop(0))
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `TreebankWordTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `span_tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that span-tokenizes untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `text` argument; a run of double-quote characters such as `'"' * n` survives to the quote branch unchanged.
3. **Path:** The branch selector at line 203 (`'"' in text` or `"''" in text`) is satisfied by the payload, entering the vulnerable branch; `matched` is built at line 205 with n entries and the reconstruction comprehension runs at line 209.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or `tokenize`. The regex timeout backstop in `nltk/redos.py` only wraps regular-expression operations and does not cover the pure-Python `list.pop(0)` sink; a 256,000-character input ran to completion in 6.57 seconds with no timeout raised.
5. **Primitive:** `matched.pop(0)` executed once per quote token, each call O(len(matched)), yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large quote-run input exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Direct inspection found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or length check in `nltk/tokenize/treebank.py`, in contrast to the sibling `sonority_sequencing.py` which does cap token length. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that `tokenize` collapses repeated quotes so few `pop(0)` calls occur was disproven by observing that `tokenize('"' * n)` yields exactly n quote tokens and timing showing about 4x growth per doubling, while an equal-token-count non-quote control ran roughly 11x faster; (2) the hypothesis that the project regex-timeout backstop already caps this cost was disproven by running a 256,000-character input to normal completion in 6.57 seconds with no `TimeoutError`, confirming the backstop wraps only regex operations and not `list.pop(0)`; (3) the hypothesis that this line was already audited was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite explicitly clears the neighboring `align_tokens` line reached through `span_tokenize` but contains no test for the `pop(0)` loop, an audited-neighbor pattern where the adjacent line was checked and this one was missed. The seed remediation touched a different module and no advisory covers this sink.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.2.5, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable `pop(0)` loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve through fresh execution. The lower bound of 3.2.5 reflects when the affected quote-restoration code shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the O(n) `list.pop(0)` pattern with an O(1) consumption strategy, for example iterating over `matched` with an index or an iterator, or using `collections.deque` with `popleft()`, so that the quote-restoration step runs in linear time overall. Additionally, consider enforcing a configurable maximum input length in `span_tokenize` consistent with the caps applied to sibling tokenizers, and ensure the fix covers all callers that pass untrusted text. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose span tokenization of untrusted input can cap request and input sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Two pull requests carry a fix.

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured). Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (the quote-restore loop in tokenize/treebank.py and tokenize/destructive.py iterates forward instead of list.pop(0)).

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144. Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)".

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run (span_tokenize over 32k and 128k double quotes): #3753 head 3.5x over a 4x input, #3895 head 3.2x, both linear. On develop 2fa3f48fe the 128k run did not finish within 120 s, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

raw.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: RBAC override configs in VirtualHost and Route resources are not applied
raw.details:
### Summary

`XdsServer` in `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` does not apply `RBACPerRoute` overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, `XdsServer` ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.

### Details

### Override parser lookup uses the override message type

`parseOverrideFilterConfig()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257

`setup()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173

The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains `parseOverrideRbacConfig()`, and server.ts silently skips the override.

### Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter name

`overrideConfigMaps` in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under `filterConfig.typeUrl`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174

Route overrides are later looked up by their `typed_per_filter_config` key, which is the `HttpFilter.name`. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.

### VirtualHost overrides are not read

`handleRouteConfigurationResource()` in server.ts:225-249 reads `route.typed_per_filter_config` but never reads `virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249

When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.

### Proof of concept

Set:
```
GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=true
```

Run `XdsServer` with a protected unary handler.

Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:

```
name: rbac
typed_config:
  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC
  rules:
    action: ALLOW
    policies:
      allow-any:
        principals: [{ any: true }]
        permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:

```
typed_per_filter_config:
  rbac:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute
    rbac:
      rules:
        action: DENY
        policies:
          deny-any:
            principals: [{ any: true }]
            permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.

Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.

Observed: `XdsServer` ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.

```
Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKED
gRPC status: OK
handler invocations: 1
response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDE
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.

raw.summary: Action Pack: Missing SameSite attribute on session cookies from Action Pack session stores
raw.details:
### Impact
Action Pack session stores other than `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` (`CacheStore`, `MemCacheStore`, and third-party stores built on `AbstractStore`, `AbstractSecureStore` or the session mixins) write the session cookie without a `SameSite` attribute, regardless of `config.action_dispatch.cookies_same_site_protection`, which defaults to `:lax`. Only `CookieStore` applies the configured policy. In browsers that do not treat a cookie without the attribute as `SameSite=Lax`, a cross-site request could carry the session cookie, possibly leading to cross-site request forgery against actions that do not verify an authenticity token, such as those of API-only applications.

Applications are affected when they use a session store other than `CookieStore` and do not pass `same_site:` to `config.session_store`.

### Details
In the fixed releases, every session store sets the session cookie's `SameSite` attribute from `cookies_same_site_protection` when its options have no `:same_site` key. An explicit `same_site:` option, including `same_site: nil`, and a `:same_site` value in a store's `DEFAULT_OPTIONS` still take precedence.

### Workarounds
Pass `same_site:` when configuring the session store, for example `config.session_store :cache_store, same_site: :lax`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2d9f502df941e31ce9bad0e846564f49396bed46.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/f2392996be723708271a8d30bfcf0edc221e53ef.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [tjvc](https://hackerone.com/tjvc).

raw.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
raw.details:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

```text
Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; the effect is availability degradation of the affected process. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is exhaustion of the available worker pool; this is inferred from the per-request cost and was not itself executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed because the quadratic behavior is driven entirely by the attacker token, not by the size of the legal-onset set.`

1. Construct a tokenizer with any small onset source.
2. Call `tokenize` with an all-vowel token of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against a consonant-alternating control token of equal length.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import LegalitySyllableTokenizer

tok = LegalitySyllableTokenizer("tr c d".split())  # tiny 3-word onset source
for n in (8000, 16000, 32000):
    payload = "a" * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    tok.tokenize(payload)
    print("vowel-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "ba" * 32000  # equal-length linear control
start = time.perf_counter()
tok.tokenize(control)
print("control", 64000, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
vowel-run 8000 0.031
vowel-run 16000 0.120
vowel-run 32000 0.468   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 64000 0.004     (linear, roughly 130x faster at larger size)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `LegalitySyllableTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that syllabifies untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `token` argument, including its length and character content; a run of vowels such as `"a" * n` survives with no normalization or length reduction.
3. **Path:** The token flows into the reverse walk at `nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py:126` and reaches the membership-test at line 133 on every iteration past the first vowel.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on this path. The sibling `SyllableTokenizer` received a `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` cap during the project hardening work, but `legality_principle.py` received no such guard.
5. **Primitive:** Repeated O(k) construction and hashing of `current_onset[::-1]` inside the loop yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large vowel-run token exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Membership-set analysis shows the first branch at line 133 cannot fire for a vowel character because `legal_onsets` is provably vowel-free (it is derived from `onset()`, which stops at the first vowel), so `onset` never becomes `True` and `current_onset` is never reset. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that the quadratic depends on a large or specific onset corpus was disproven by reproducing the same O(n^2) growth with a three-word onset source, showing the cost is driven solely by the attacker token; (2) the hypothesis that an upstream length cap neutralizes long tokens was disproven by direct source inspection, which found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or equivalent clamp on this class and confirmed the default word-tokenization path does not call this class; (3) the hypothesis that this is covered by existing hardening was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite exercises the sibling `SyllableTokenizer` but contains no test for `LegalitySyllableTokenizer`, and no commit added a cap to this file. This is a fix-missed sibling of the accepted algorithmic-complexity class, not a previously remediated issue.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.6, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve. The lower bound of 3.6 reflects when the affected module first shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a bound on per-token work in `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize`, consistent with the `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` guard already applied to the sibling `SyllableTokenizer`. Options include rejecting or truncating tokens above a configurable maximum length before the reverse walk, or restructuring the onset accumulation so the loop does not repeatedly build and hash a growing reversed string (for example by maintaining the onset in its final orientation and comparing without an O(k) reversal each iteration). The remediation should cover any caller that passes untrusted tokens, not just the default word-tokenization path. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose syllabification of untrusted input can cap request and token sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case token length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144.

Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)" (LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize refuses a token longer than MAX_TOKEN_LEN=4096 with ValueError naming CWE-407).

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run: on the PR head the 32k vowel token is refused and under the cap the tokenizer scales 0.8x over a 4x input (1k vs 4k); on develop 2fa3f48fe it scales 14.2x over a 4x input (8k 0.087 s, 32k 1.245 s), so develop is still VULNERABLE. The related merged PR #3911 (25beee962) bounds the SyllableTokenizer vowel accumulation, a different tokenizer, and does not cover this sink.

raw.summary: AutoMapper: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion that bypasses MaxDepth
raw.details:
### Summary
The default and explicit `MaxDepth` limits added for CVE-2026-32933 don't apply to several mapping paths. Mapping a deeply nested source through any of them recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`, which can't be caught and terminates the process.

### Affected paths
- **Polymorphic maps:** derived type maps (`Include` / `IncludeBase`) didn't inherit the base map's `MaxDepth`, and the default limit for self-referential maps was only applied to the base map. A chain of derived objects was mapped without a limit, even with `MaxDepth` set on the base map.
- **Runtime-typed members:** members typed as `object` or an interface aren't seen by self-reference detection, so the default limit isn't applied.
- **Dictionary and dynamic sources:** mapping a nested `Dictionary<string, object>` or `ExpandoObject` (for example, deserialized JSON) onto typed destinations recurses with no depth tracking. `MaxDepth` has no effect.
- **Recursive type converters:** `ConvertUsing` that calls `context.Mapper.Map` ignores `MaxDepth`.

### Impact
An application that maps attacker-influenced, deeply nested data through one of these paths can be crashed. On a 1 MB stack (the Windows default), a few thousand levels of nesting are enough.

### Fix
- Derived type maps inherit `MaxDepth`, and the default limit is applied to them.
- Every runtime map call checks for sufficient stack, and fails with a catchable `InsufficientExecutionStackException` instead of overflowing.

### Workarounds
Set `MaxDepth` explicitly on derived maps and on maps reached through `object` or interface members. There is no configuration workaround for dictionary or dynamic sources, or for recursive type converters, other than limiting input depth before mapping.

### Related
- CVE-2026-32933 (GHSA-rvv3-g6hj-g44x)
- GHSA-6vhm-j9h7-f9gh: `MaxDepth` not enforced through constructor parameters and positional records, fixed in the same releases.

raw.summary: code16/sharp: Arbitrary class instantiation through the embed_key API parameter

An authenticated attacker can instantiate any class in the PHP application by using the `embed_key` parameter across multiple API endpoints. The instantiation is performed by the Laravel container. raw.summary: Loofah: Mutation XSS in the HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
raw.details:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<` and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip` scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values, as the HTML standard requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

## Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API (`Loofah.html5_fragment`, `Loofah.html5_document` and the `scrub_html5_*` methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with the default allowlist.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including `Loofah::Helpers.sanitize`), the `:whitewash` scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and JRuby.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

raw.summary: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
raw.details:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

### Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as `{[0-9]*}`, with `UnsupportedPathError`. `PreparedRegExpRouter` data must be regenerated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default `SmartRouter`, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Use `new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() })`.

raw.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
raw.details:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=` set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible circumvention of file size limits in Active Storage direct uploads to Google Cloud Storage
raw.details:
### Impact
`ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` does not bind the declared content length into the signed direct-upload URL, and `#headers_for_direct_upload` returns no length constraint, so the URL authorizes an upload body of any size. A direct-upload client could store a file larger than the `byte_size` it declared, and the resulting blob keeps the declared size, possibly bypassing application file size validations and quotas. This is the weakness that CVE-2020-8162 fixed in the S3 service.

Applications that store files in Google Cloud Storage and accept direct uploads are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign an `x-goog-content-length-range` header that matches the blob's declared `byte_size` and return it from `headers_for_direct_upload`, so Cloud Storage rejects an upload body of any other size. Browsers send this header with the direct upload, so a bucket's CORS configuration must list `x-goog-content-length-range` in `responseHeader`, or browser direct uploads fail after the upgrade. The Active Storage CHANGELOG and the CORS example in the Active Storage guide show the change.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e19916cea31cbfb0030b165ae853b741f8dd57a7.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7fe85a72a789eae5ee070ce3ee1dad10a8a5f70c.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [f4cts](https://hackerone.com/f4cts).

raw.summary: compose-lint: Text in a pull request can issue CI workflow commands through JSON and SARIF output on stdout
raw.details:
### Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. `--format json` and `--format sarif` output never passed through that fix, so `##[` inside a service name or other value reaches the log intact when the output is printed to stdout rather than written to a file. The runner acts on `##[` in the middle of a line, so the JSON layout does not prevent it.

A pull request can therefore create annotations, fold or hide parts of the job log, or issue other commands the runner accepts, when CI runs compose-lint over it, before anyone reviews it. The pass/fail result is not changed.

Affected setups print JSON or SARIF output to a CI log from the `compose-lint` package, the pre-commit hook or the Docker image. Writing that output to a file, which SARIF upload requires, is not affected. The GitHub Action turns command processing off around each compose-lint run, so it is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review. It was first published as part of GHSA-r7j4-crjv-h467, together with four other gaps in the same fix. Each gap now has its own advisory.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tag 0.31.0 and the matching minor tag are affected, as was `latest` while it pointed to 0.31.0.

Releases before 0.31.0 are covered by GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. JSON and SARIF on stdout escape `##[` inside strings as `\u005b`, which decodes to the same data.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
- Write `--format json` and `--format sarif` output to a file rather than the log.
- On GitHub Actions, use the `tmatens/compose-lint` Action, or bracket the compose-lint step with `::stop-commands::<random token>` and `::<token>::`, as the Action does.

### Reproduction

On compose-lint 0.31.0 on a GitHub-hosted runner (runner 2.337.0), a service named `a##[warning]X`, linted with `--format json` or `--format sarif` to stdout, creates annotations. The same file linted with the text report creates none. The `composelint/compose-lint:0.31.0` image produces byte-identical output to the package.

raw.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with certain exploded expressions
raw.details:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is only exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. MRI Ruby 3.2 and later are not affected: their regular expression engine memoizes backtracking, so these patterns still match in linear time. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected either. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Not affected |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.2 or later, if the consuming application does not use JRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates that use the `*` modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported independently by @ebenoist, @andrewstellman, and then @halogenandtoast.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session
raw.details:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `connection.process()` when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a `close_notify` alert or a call to `close()`, or before `handshake()` is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`tls.handleHandshake()` in `lib/tls.js` updates the handshake digests with `c.session.md5.update(bytes)` before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in `handshake()`, and `c.reset()` sets it to `null` when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches `handleHandshake()`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')`.

This happens:
- after the server sends a `close_notify` alert (at any alert level);
- after the application calls `close()`;
- before the application calls `handshake()`.

The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` from a `data` event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.

Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.

The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to `process()` once the `closed` callback has been called and until `handshake()` is called again.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client `TypeError`, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-use.

### Proof of concept
    var c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});
    c.handshake();
    // warning close_notify alert, then an empty ServerHello, in separate
    // process() calls
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('15030100020100'));
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('160301000402000000'));
    // <= 1.4.2: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')
    // 1.4.3: the record is ignored

The reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-j8rw-jp99-435v.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

raw.summary: Loofah allowed_uri? treats data:text/html as safe text/plain
raw.details:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `data:` URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference `/` in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed `text/plain`, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as `text/html`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` decodes HTML entities with `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. `/` therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no `/`, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed `text/plain` under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

`:`, `/`, `	` and `
` are the only named character references in the HTML5 table that decode to characters that change how a URI parses (U+003A, U+002F, U+0009 and U+000A; there is no named reference for U+000D), so this closes the set.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @ngpestelos.
